slides.say: Given: x is a prime number, and x to the power of six is a two-digit number. What is nine x?

So x is a prime, and its sixth power has only two digits. That's a big hint, because a sixth power grows really fast, so x must be a small number. And look, they don't ask for x, they ask for nine x. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, trial and error first, and then plugging in the answers.

[short pause] Our first method, trial and error. Remember, with primes we can simply try numbers against the conditions. And x is a prime, so we only try primes. Which one first? The smallest prime, two, because a small x gives a small power.
Two to the power of six. Two times two is four, times two is eight, times two is sixteen, times two is thirty-two, and times two is sixty-four. Sixty-four has two digits, so two fits.
at: Two to the power of six

slides.say: Can I already stop? Not yet, because maybe another prime fits too. So the next prime, three. Three times three is nine, times three is twenty-seven. That's three to the power of three, and it has two digits, but careful, we need the power of six. Twenty-seven times three is eighty-one, and eighty-one times three is two hundred forty-three. That's only the power of five, and it already has three digits.
at: we need the power of six

slides.say: One more three. Two hundred forty-three times three, two hundred times three is six hundred, and forty-three times three is a hundred twenty-nine. Together, seven hundred twenty-nine. Three digits, so three is out.
And what does that mean for five, seven and all the bigger primes? A bigger base gives a bigger power. So if three is already too big, every bigger prime is too big too. So x is two.

Now careful, because x isn't the answer. A lot of students find that x is two, and go looking for two in the choices. They ask for nine x. Nine times two is eighteen, so choice number two is our answer.
at: choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Our second method, plugging in the answers. Each choice is nine x, so to get x back, I divide the choice by nine. Twenty-seven over nine is three, eighteen over nine is two, sixty-three over nine is seven, and forty-five over nine is five.
Are they primes? Three, two, seven and five, yes, all four. So the prime condition doesn't rule anything out here, and the power has to decide.

Choice number one gives x is three. Three, nine, twenty-seven, eighty-one, two hundred forty-three, and seven hundred twenty-nine. That's three to the power of six, and it has three digits, so choice number one is out.
Choice numbers three and four give seven and five. They're bigger than three, so their powers are even bigger. Both out.
And choice number two gives x is two. Two to the power of six is sixty-four, two digits. It works, so choice number two is our answer.
So when a power has only a few digits, start trying from the smallest prime. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
